title: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
summary: Describes an updated version of the security architecture for IP, which provides security services for traffic at the IP layer. It explains how IPsec components fit together and replaces RFC 2401. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: IPsec is a guard built into the internet's addressing layer. This memo is the blueprint showing how all its parts work together to keep messages private and honest.

subtitle: The blueprint for IPsec: how security associations and three databases decide which IP packets get protected, dropped or passed through.

tldr.problem: IP by itself offers no protection. Hosts and gateways need a standard way to authenticate, protect and filter traffic at the IP layer for IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: IPsec places a boundary between protected and unprotected sides. A policy database decides per packet whether to PROTECT, DISCARD or BYPASS. Protected traffic travels over security associations that use ESP or AH.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4301 obsoletes RFC 2401. It is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 6040 and RFC 7619.

today: RFC 4301 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2401. It has been updated by RFC 6040 and RFC 7619, and it updates RFC 3168.

sections.title: Goals of the IPsec Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 4301 specifies the base architecture for IPsec-compliant systems. It describes the requirements for systems that implement IPsec, the fundamental elements of such systems, and how they fit together and into the IP environment, for both IPv4 and IPv6. Other RFCs define the individual protocols and algorithms.

The security services are access control, connectionless integrity, data origin authentication, detection and rejection of replays, confidentiality through encryption, and limited traffic flow confidentiality. They work at the IP layer, so they protect every protocol carried over IP. The spelling IPsec is the preferred one.

IPsec includes minimal firewall functionality, since that is an essential part of access control at the IP layer. The protocols are designed to be independent of cryptographic algorithms. The default algorithms are specified in separate documents, so they can be updated without reopening the architecture.

The RFC is honest about limits. This is not a security architecture for the Internet, only for the IP layer. The security achieved also depends on the quality of the implementation and on the operating environment.
sections.eli5: IPsec puts the locks on the delivery trucks themselves, so every kind of package inside gets protected, whatever it is.

sections.title: How IPsec Works: Boundary, Protocols and Placement
sections.content:
An IPsec implementation sits in a host, in a security gateway (SG) such as an IPsec-enabled firewall or router, or in an independent device. It creates a boundary between unprotected and protected interfaces. Each packet crossing it is matched against the Security Policy Database (SPD) using selectors and gets one of three actions: PROTECT using IPsec, DISCARD, or BYPASS IPsec protection.

Two protocols provide protection. The Authentication Header (AH) offers integrity and data origin authentication with optional anti-replay. The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) offers the same and also confidentiality. Implementations MUST support ESP and MAY support AH, because experience showed that ESP can provide the needed services in nearly all contexts. ESP confidentiality without integrity is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Implementation can be native in the IP stack, bump-in-the-stack (BITS) beneath an existing stack, or bump-in-the-wire (BITW) as a dedicated inline processor. The document assumes IKEv2, or a key management system with comparable features.
sections.eli5: The guard looks at each visitor and picks one of three things: seal the envelope, turn them away, or wave them through. Two types of seals exist, and one does everything the other does and more.

sections.title: Security Associations and Modes
sections.content:
A Security Association (SA) is a simplex connection that provides security services to the traffic it carries, using AH or ESP but not both. Two-way communication therefore needs a pair of SAs, one per direction, and IKE creates such pairs. For unicast, the 32-bit Security Parameters Index (SPI) by itself can identify an SA. Multicast needs a defined lookup order: SPI plus destination and source addresses, then SPI plus destination, then SPI alone or SPI and protocol.

An SA is in one of two modes. In transport mode the security header sits right after the IP header and protects the next layer protocol. ESP in this mode does not cover the IP header. In tunnel mode the SA is applied to an IP tunnel, with an outer header naming the tunnel endpoints and an inner header naming the original sender and recipient. When either end is a security gateway, the SA MUST be tunnel mode, with two exceptions, such as traffic addressed to the gateway itself.

Traffic of different classes that match the same selectors should go on different SAs when anti-replay is used. Otherwise the anti-replay window could wrongly discard lower priority packets. The RFC also notes that AH and ESP cannot be applied in transport mode to IPv4 fragments.
sections.eli5: An SA is a one-way sealed tube between two places. For talking back and forth you need two tubes, one for each direction.

sections.title: The Three IPsec Databases
sections.content:
The SPD is an ordered policy database. Each entry names a disposition (PROTECT, BYPASS or DISCARD) and is keyed by selectors. The selectors include local and remote IP address ranges, next layer protocol, and ports, ICMP type and code or Mobility Header type when relevant. Values can be a range, ANY or OPAQUE when a field is unavailable, as in a non-initial fragment. The SPD is logically divided into SPD-S (secure traffic), SPD-I (inbound bypass or discard) and SPD-O (outbound bypass or discard). Every SPD SHOULD end with a final entry that discards anything unmatched.

The Security Association Database (SAD) holds the parameters of each SA. These include the SPI, a sequence number counter (64-bit by default), an anti-replay window, algorithms and keys, lifetime by time and byte count, mode, and path MTU. For inbound packets, the SAD also acts as a cache for checking that header fields match the selectors negotiated for the SA.

The Peer Authorization Database (PAD) links the SPD to a key management protocol such as IKE. It identifies authorized peers, says how each is authenticated and with what data, and limits which identities a peer may assert when child SAs are created.
sections.eli5: The guard has three notebooks. One holds the rules, one holds the details of every sealed tube already built, and one lists who is allowed to ask for a new tube.

sections.title: SA and Key Management
sections.content:
All IPsec implementations MUST support both manual and automated SA and key management. Manual keying means a person configures keying material by hand. It works for small, static settings but does not scale. Automated management is required to use anti-replay and to create SAs on demand. Rekeying an SA means creating a new SA with a new SPI.

The default automated protocol is IKEv2. Other automated protocols MAY be used. One negotiation yields several keys for an SA, and a minimum of four are needed if both integrity and confidentiality are used, because each direction has its own SA. When a single bit string is split into keys, encryption keys MUST come from the first (left-most, high-order) bits and integrity keys from the remaining bits.
sections.eli5: Keys can be handed out by hand, which is fine for a few friends, or by a trusted process that scales to many. Either way, both ends must cut the key into the same pieces.

sections.title: Processing Outbound and Inbound Traffic
sections.content:
For outbound packets, IPsec picks the right SPD through an SPD selection function, matches the packet against the SPD cache, and acts on the entry. A cache miss means a search of the SPD. If the entry says PROTECT and no SA exists, the key management mechanism, such as IKEv2, is invoked to create one. If creation fails, the packet is discarded. The packet then goes to the forwarding function, which may loop it back across the boundary for nested processing, and that needs a matching SPD-I entry.

For inbound packets, traffic that looks IPsec protected and is addressed to the device is mapped to an SA through the SAD using the SPI. Everything else goes to an SPD-I lookup. IKE traffic MUST have an explicit BYPASS entry.

For tunnel mode, the outer header addresses identify the tunnel endpoints and the inner header is left unchanged apart from fields such as TTL and the DS and ECN fields. IPsec tunnel mode differs from plain IP-in-IP tunneling by adding controls for covert channels. The RFC also covers ICMP error handling, fragments on the protected side, and path MTU and DF bit processing in later sections. It describes auditing as not required, with minimum audit information given for certain events.
sections.eli5: Going out, the guard checks the rulebook, builds a sealed tube if one is needed, and sends the packet through. Coming in, the guard reads the label on the tube to know which key opens it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security permeates the whole specification. IPsec imposes strict limits on what header data may pass across the boundary in either direction, particularly with tunnel mode. Outbound, the limits reduce covert channel bandwidth. Inbound, they stop an attacker who can tamper with one data stream on the unprotected side from harming other streams on the protected side.

The RFC gives one concrete warning about ICMP error messages. Suppose sites A, B and C are connected by ESP tunnels whose selectors specify ANY for protocol and ports. If ICMP errors are passed over SAs based on the ICMP header alone, a host at site B could send a Destination Unreachable message declaring all hosts at site C unreachable. That is an efficient denial-of-service attack, preventable by checking ICMP errors as Section 6.2 describes. Section 9 adds that a receiver need not reply to the purported sender when it detects an auditable event, because replying could itself induce denial of service.
sections.eli5: If the guard believed any note that said 'that street is closed', a troublemaker could close the whole town. So notes must be checked like everything else.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2401
sections.content:
RFC 4301 differs substantially from RFC 2401 in detail and organization, but the fundamental notions are unchanged. Key changes include a revised processing model with separate SPD caches for outbound and inbound bypassed or discarded traffic, and the new Peer Authorization Database.

Nested SAs and SA bundles are no longer required, because the same effect can be achieved through SPD and forwarding table configuration. SPD entries were redefined to carry lists of ranges. TOS and Traffic Class were replaced by DSCP and ECN. Support for AH is no longer required. Transport mode may now be used between gateways, and between a gateway and a host. Section 7 gives three approaches for plaintext fragments on the protected side, and an ICMP message type and code and the Mobility Header type were added as selectors. The selector 'data sensitivity level' was removed.
sections.eli5: This is the new edition of the rulebook. It keeps the same ideas but tidies up how the guard works and drops some old rules.
